overview.text: Still-life painting is a genre centered on inanimate things from nature or human making—such as fruit, flowers, game, bowls, books, and tableware. Artists select and arrange these objects, then use composition, light, color, and surface detail to make them feel vivid and expressive. The genre became an independent specialty in the Netherlands in the early 1600s, amid growing interest in domestic life, trade, and possessions. Still lifes can celebrate beauty and skill, but objects such as skulls, fading flowers, or clocks may also suggest death and how quickly pleasures pass. From Dutch flower and banquet pictures to Cézanne’s experiments with form and perspective, artists have used the genre for varied purposes.

key_facts.text: Still lifes show inanimate objects, including foods, flowers, vessels, and other natural or human-made things.
Arranging objects lets artists explore composition, perspective, light, shadow, texture, and color.
Still-life painting flourished as an independent specialty in the Netherlands in the early 1600s; related motifs appeared in European religious art earlier.
Some still lifes use symbols such as skulls, hourglasses, or wilting flowers to evoke death and life’s transience; meanings depend on the particular work.

The genre is not limited to realistic pictures of fruit: artists have used still-life subjects to test new techniques and styles, including Cézanne’s experiments with objects’ shapes, colors, lighting, and placement.
